articles.title: Victims of Pennsylvania mass shooting included gunman’s pregnant daughter
articles.summary: Matthew Stone, 45, opened fire at his home in Erie, killing eight people, before turning the gun on himself, according to the county coroner.
articles.body: The victims of a mass shooting in northwest Pennsylvania included the gunman’s wife and pregnant daughter, who was due to give birth Monday, authorities said. Matthew Stone, 45, died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound Friday after he opened fire at his home on Perry Street in Erie, Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook told NBC News on Monday. Victims included Stone’s wife, Michelle Stone, 44; daughter, Angelina K. Stone, 24, who was pregnant; and sons Matthew Stone Jr., 21, and Jonathan Stone, 19, Cook said. Angelina Stone was carrying “an unborn fetus who was supposed to have been born today,” Cook said. Two other unidentified children, a 5-year-old boy and a nearly 2-year-old girl, who were also related to the shooter were killed inside the house, according to the coroner. All six of those victims were found in the house, where they lived, while victims Twila A. Tanner, 51, and Lora Lee Roberts, 37, were fatally shot outside, Cook said. Roberts was Michelle Stone’s sister and had gone to the house Friday at the request of Angelina Stone, who needed a ride to the hospital, said the victim’s friend Christine Tombaugh. Tanner was a friend and neighbor of Roberts, and they lived just a few miles from the crime scene, Tombaugh said. Roberts was active in local homeless advocacy work, so answering a relative’s call for help and bringing along a friend for assistance was typical of her kindness, Tombaugh said. “Absolutely, that’s who she was,” said Tombaugh, executive director of the homeless shelter Community of Caring. “Her passion in life was helping others. She had a giving spirit, a beautiful heart,” Tombaugh said. “Great mom, just a valued friend. She had a heart for the homeless and people in need, just helping whoever she could. That was her passion.” Juicesiyah Alexander Ezekiel, the slain girl’s father, said he is struggling to understand why the elder Stone opened fire. “I wouldn’t even put this on my worst enemy, man,” Ezekiel told NBC affiliate WICU of Erie. “It’s sickening.” The girl was going to turn 2 next month. “Her name is Amari’anna,” Ezekiel said. “She’s the most beautiful baby God could have created.”

articles.title: Public inquiry over Manchester synagogue attack deaths
articles.summary: The Home Secretary confirms a public inquiry will examine Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby's deaths.
articles.body:
A public inquiry will examine the deaths of two men killed during an attack at a synagogue in Manchester.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from multiple stab wounds and fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, tried to get in the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October 2025.

Announcing the inquiry, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "What happened that day must be fully understood."

Syrian-born UK citizen Al-Shamie was shot dead by police while he carried out his attack.

Police had already seized Al-Shamie's mobile phone containing details of his extremist mindset but did not analyse the contents until after he had attacked the synagogue.

It took place on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for Jews.

Mahmood said: "In recent days, we marked the first anniversary of the terror attack at the Heaton Park synagogue.

"On that awful day in October of last year, as our Jewish community celebrated Yom Kippur, two brave men – Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby – lost their lives, and three others were seriously injured.

"What happened that day must be fully understood. So, as requested by the coroner, I can today announce a public inquiry into the deaths of Mr Cravitz and Mr Daulby.

"This will ensure that all evidence can be heard, including any sensitive national security material that could not otherwise be fully heard in the coroner's court."

Earlier this year a police chief said he was "deeply sorry" over missed opportunities to potentially uncover the plot to attack the synagogue.

The apology came after details emerged following the jailing of Al-Shamie's friend and accomplice, Mohammad Bashir, 31, who was sentenced to life imprisonment in July at Manchester Crown Court for planning a separate attack with Al-Shamie on the UK Defence Academy at Shrivenham.

After the hearing, Sir Stephen Watson, Chief Constable of Greater Manchester Police (GMP), said: "It is factually the case that Al-Shamie had come to the notice of GMP in respect of two linked criminal allegations which did not relate to terrorist offences.

"These allegations resulted in his being arrested on the 13 February 2025 on suspicion of breaching a non-molestation order; and on the 21 September 2025 on suspicion of rape.

"At the time of his committing the attack at the Heaton Park Synagogue, Al-Shamie was on police bail."

Watson added: "In conducting an internal review, it became apparent that GMP had seized Al-Shamie's mobile devices, at the point of each arrest.

"The significance of the data contents of these devices was substantial in respect of evidencing an extremist mindset.

"Regrettably, I can confirm that the significance of the information stored on Al-Shamie's devices was not realised, as they had not been examined before the attack took place on the 2 October 2025.

"There can, however, be little doubt that the information contained within these devices would have inspired further investigative action.

"It is clear that our not having reviewed the data available to us prior to the attack constitutes a missed opportunity."

He added: "I am disappointed at the prospect of adding to the distress of all of those affected by the terrible events last October.

"It is my fervent hope and expectation that the continuing independent reviews and processes will be able to draw together all the available evidence such as to leave no question unanswered."

At an earlier hearing the same month, Home Office lawyers applied to withhold some information from MI5 being made public at a future inquest due to national security concerns.

articles.title: Egypt’s press union chief rejects pressure over detained journalists
articles.summary: Six journalists from independent platform Matsadaash allege torture in detention, which Egypt denies.
articles.body:
The head of Egypt’s Journalists Syndicate has insisted the organisation will continue to fight for press freedom after it came under fire for defending six journalists who were detained last month and charged with joining a “terrorist” group.

“What happens to one colleague affects us all, and may happen to others tomorrow,” Khaled Elbalshy said in a statement on Sunday. “An infringement of one journalist’s freedom is an infringement of everyone’s freedom and a weakening of the safeguards protecting that freedom.”

His comments came after the syndicate filed a complaint with Egypt’s public prosecutor over allegations that the detained journalists, who work for the investigative website Matsadaash, had been tortured. Egyptian authorities denied the accusations, while pro-government commentators criticised the organisation for defending the journalists.

Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadry were arrested on September 28 and 29 and have since appeared before the Supreme State Security Prosecution, which prosecutes national security cases. They have been ordered to be held in pretrial detention for 15 days pending investigations.

Egyptian prosecutors have accused the six journalists of working for a media organisation tied to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group Egyptian authorities have cracked down on for years following a 2013 coup against democratically elected Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who was a member. Egypt has officially designated the Muslim Brotherhood as a “terrorist” group, an allegation the organisation has strongly denied, while human rights groups have accused Egyptian authorities of repressing freedoms.

Matsadaash co-founder Abdelrahman Mansour has also rejected any links between the media platform and the Muslim Brotherhood.

In his statement, Elbalshy said: “The fundamental principle governing all such matters, particularly when dealing with accused persons in general and vulnerable people in particular, remains that an accused person is innocent until proven guilty.”

The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six journalists, said they were initially held for five days without any contact with their families or lawyers. After complaints, the journalists appeared before prosecutors and were questioned in the presence of their lawyers and a representative from the Journalists Syndicate.

The EIPR said the journalists were being held under Egypt’s 2015 Counterterrorism Law that allows for suspects to be held in custody before appearing before prosecutors “when there is a risk of a terrorist crime and a necessity to confront that risk”. The rights group, however, noted that the prosecution only alleges that the journalists published rumours or “false” reports.

“The public prosecution should have identified the imminent terrorist threat that required denying them their right to appear before a judicial authority within 24 hours of their arrest,” the EIPR said on October 7.

The EIPR has also said that most of the six journalists said they were tortured following their arrests, including being beaten and subjected to electric shocks. It added that several of the detained had been forced to record fabricated confessions.

Egypt’s Interior Ministry has rejected the allegations.

Matsadaash was founded in 2018 as a fact-checking platform, but has since expanded into investigative journalism. Its website is blocked in Egypt, but it has more than 1.3 million followers on Facebook.

The outlet has previously faced pressure from Egyptian authorities, including in 2023, when one of its journalists, Karim Asaad, was arrested after Matsadaash published an investigation into a suspected smuggling scandal involving a plane that had flown from Cairo to Zambia. He was later released.

articles.title: In 2017, a Washington couple bought property with an old wooden tower; after it was replaced by a 120-foot steel tower, they say the utility threatened to cut power unless they signed an easement
articles.summary: A Washington couple’s dispute with a local utility has raised questions about property rights, infrastructure easements and the extent to which homeowners
articles.body: A Washington couple’s dispute with a local utility has raised questions about property rights, infrastructure easements and the extent to which homeowners can challenge equipment installed on their land. Liz Covert and Denis Goudie, who purchased their property in 2017, are challenging the replacement of an existing wooden tower with a taller steel structure by the Orcas Power and Light Cooperative (OPALCO). The case was reported by Moneywise on October 10, 2026, following earlier coverage by The Journal of the San Juan Islands and reporting by NBC affiliate KING 5. The couple alleges that OPALCO threatened to disconnect their electricity unless they signed an easement within 90 days, escalating a disagreement over the utility’s rights to use the property. The dispute centres on whether the existing easement permits the infrastructure now standing on the site.Dispute over an existing easementCovert and Goudie say the easement associated with their property allows landscaping-related activities but does not authorise above-ground utility infrastructure of this kind. They were aware of an older wooden tower when they purchased the land, but say they were not informed about its replacement before construction began. According to the reporting, the original structure was replaced in 2023 with a taller steel tower and a larger generator. The couple has raised concerns about additional noise during the generator’s startup cycles, as well as the tower’s impact on the surrounding landscape and views.OPALCO has offered a different account. In an October 7 statement on its website, the cooperative said the pole site had been established with the previous owner’s permission before Covert and Goudie purchased the property. The utility also argued that its members agree to grant easements when joining the cooperative, allowing it to install and maintain infrastructure where the relevant agreements permit. However, OPALCO acknowledged that easements differ in scope and that its rights depend on what each agreement allows. There is also a discrepancy over the structure’s height. While Moneywise describes it as a 120-foot tower, OPALCO says the replacement structure stands 103 feet tall, approximately 20 feet higher than its predecessor.Neighbours have raised similar concernsThe disagreement is not limited to Covert and Goudie. According to The Journal of the San Juan Islands, their neighbours, Norma and George Andreadis, are pursuing a similar legal challenge against the utility. The cases highlight a broader question for property owners: when an infrastructure easement already exists, how much authority does it give a utility to replace or upgrade equipment without obtaining fresh consent?The answer can depend on the precise language of the recorded easement, the rights granted by the previous owner and the applicable property laws. An agreement allowing access to maintain existing equipment does not necessarily settle every question about replacing it with a larger structure. The dispute is now moving through litigation, with the scope of the easement expected to be central to the case.Could a nearby tower affect property values?Beyond the legal disagreement, homeowners may also worry about the effect of telecommunications infrastructure on their property’s appearance, privacy and resale prospects. A 2019 study published in Empirical Economics Letters, examining home sales in Savannah, Georgia, found that properties within 500 feet of cellular towers sold at discounts of up to 7.6% in the dataset studied. The researchers also found that the negative association was stronger during periods of declining housing prices. The findings relate to a particular market and do not establish that every home near a tower will lose value.For homeowners concerned about a nearby structure, documenting changes to views, noise levels and the property’s surroundings can help establish the nature of the impact. Independent valuations and advice from real estate professionals may also help owners assess whether the infrastructure affects their home’s marketability.When an easement becomes a point of contentionOPALCO says easements are essential to maintaining electricity and internet services across Washington’s San Juan Islands. The member-owned, non-profit cooperative argues that allowing infrastructure to cross private land helps it serve the wider community without imposing additional costs on members. For Covert and Goudie, however, the central issue is whether the permissions attached to their property extend to the upgraded structure and whether the utility can require them to accept a new agreement. The outcome could turn on the wording of the original easement and the legal rights available to both sides. articles.title: UK blames Iran for airbase plot, sanctions two Iranian nationals
articles.summary: Iran’s ambassador tells UK officials Tehran willing to assist in investigation, reiterates denial of involvement.
articles.body:
Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that a suspected plot targeting Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), raising the diplomatic stakes over the largely unexplained incident for which Tehran has denied any responsibility.

“We will not tolerate these threats on our soil,” Burnham told parliament on Monday, adding that the government, “will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams”.

“We will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm”, he said.

The incident near the airbase in southern England occurred in the early hours of September 27 when five British men in their 20s were arrested on suspected “terrorism” and explosives offences.

Police said they found a supply of petrol in three vans linked to the suspects, but no explosives.

They were later released without charge on ‌‌‌‌police ⁠⁠⁠⁠bail “under stringent conditions”. Last week, Counter Terrorism Policing arrested a 22-year-old British national on suspicion of a “terror” offence linked to the security incident. Earlier this month, a 25-year-old British-Iranian man was arrested in London.

In a statement on X, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Britain was sanctioning two Iranians for their “role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime”, without specifying their identity.

“We have repeatedly made clear to Iran, Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil”, he said.

The move came as 29 countries, including Britain, the US, most European states, Canada, Australia and New Zealand issued a joint statement on Monday blaming Iran for the attempted infiltration.

“Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable”, it said.

On Monday, Ali Mousavi, Iran’s ambassador to the UK, met Stephen Doughty, the UK’s minister for the Middle East, and “categorically rejected” allegations of any Iranian role while urging “the British side to refrain from any unsubstantiated statements”.

Mousavi told British authorities that Tehran is willing to cooperate with the investigation into the incident , Iran’s ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠state news agency IRNA reported.

Iran’s embassy in London issued a statement last month saying Iran “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” attempting to link the country to the arrests, adding that it will “fuel Iranophobia propaganda”.

The US moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from the base earlier this month.

RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war against Iran, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.

Located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, RAF Fairford is the preferred European base for US bombers. Their withdrawal was made over concerns about a suspected Iranian plot to carry out a complex drone attack on the facility, according to US officials.

articles.title: US actress Selma Blair accused of assault after incident with flight attendants
articles.summary: The Legally Blonde star is investigated by the FBI following an alleged altercation on a flight from LA to New York.
articles.body:
US actress Selma Blair has been issued with a summons accusing her of assault after she allegedly attacked attendants on a plane, officials say.

The Legally Blonde star was investigated by the FBI following an alleged altercation on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York.

Airport officials said they had responded to a call on Sunday about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.

Blair, 54, who also starred in Hellboy and Cruel Intentions, was arrested and taken to hospital. Her publicist told the BBC she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".

"Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition," her publicist said.

On Monday, a federal law enforcement source told the BBC that Blair had been issued a summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US.

The source said she will be required to appear at the petty violation court in Brooklyn, New York City, but no date has been set.

The incident occurred around 23:00 local time aboard Delta Airlines Flight 938.

According to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the flight crew allegedly restrained Blair on the flight. Air traffic control audio obtained by CBS includes the pilot calling for medical personnel to come to the plane, citing a "bloody nose as well as some bite marks".

A spokesperson for Delta Air Lines said that law enforcement responded as the flight arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York, and that there was no operational impact to the flight because of the incident.

"Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," Delta Air Lines said in a statement to the BBC.

Blair largely retreated from film work amid her 2018 multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis , telling the BBC years later that she blamed the disease for taking "my career down" because "I had to stop working".

In 2021, she announced she was in remission for the disease.

In 2016, she had another incident on a flight after a drunken outburst caused two nurses to have to subdue her on board.

Blair issued a public apology after the incident. She said she accidentally mixed her medication with alcohol and "made a big mistake" that caused her to "black out" and "say and do things that I deeply regret".

"I am a flawed human being who makes mistakes and am filled with shame over this incident. I am truly very sorry," she said at the time.

US media reported at the time that the actress was screaming uncontrollably and that nurses had to prop her up with a pillow and give her oxygen to calm down.

She was taken off the plane on a stretcher when the flight landed in Los Angeles from Mexico, and was taken to hospital.

articles.title: Zelensky unleashes on Trump as Russia diesel deal rallies Ukraine’s supporters
articles.summary: Kyiv’s allies, including those in President Trump’s circle, are rallying around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, pushing back against Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and threats to cut off weapons and intelligence sharing to Ukraine. Zelensky, buoyed by the support, has unleashed criticism against Trump, calling the president “weak” for making a deal with Russian President…
articles.body:
Kyiv’s allies, including those in President Trump’s circle, are rallying around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, pushing back against Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and threats to cut off weapons and intelligence sharing to Ukraine.

Zelensky, buoyed by the support, has unleashed criticism against Trump, calling the president “weak” for making a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. And he’s challenging Trump’s narrative over high diesel prices, pointing to the U.S. war with Iran as the main driver.

“Everybody understands that the prices of diesel, it doesn’t depend on our attacks on diesel in Russia,” Zelensky said in an interview on America’s Newsroom on Fox News, addressing Trump’s favorite news channel during the morning hours, when he’s reportedly most likely to be watching.

“Everybody understands that it depends on the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.”

Zelensky’s indignation followed Trump’s announcement on Friday that he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an effort to lower prices in the U.S. — promoting the deal as a salve before the midterms as American voters fret over the cost of living.

Trump’s diesel deal drew immediate and wide-ranging pushback from Ukraine’s supporters.

Fox News host Mark Levin, who has a direct line to the president, said Putin is the actual obstacle to achieving peace in Eastern Europe and highlighted the Kremlin’s support for Iran in its conflict against the U.S.

“Putin started the war. Putin has refused all peace deals with absurd demands or outright rejection. Putin has caused the death of 1 million or more,” Levin wrote Monday morning on the social platform X. “Putin has nuclear missiles aimed at our country. Putin is providing support to the Iranian regime.”

Levin echoed the view coming from other people Trump pays attention to, like Fox News host Brian Kilmeade, who threw down over the weekend with co-host Rachel Campos-Duffy — who is married to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy — as she backed Trump’s criticism of Zelensky.

“It would be the biggest mistake of his administration to work with Russia,” Kilmeade said, speaking about the president.

“That is the modern Hitler of our generation,” he added of Putin. “He is the cause of all the problems in the region, and now, is helping Iran kill our guys and blow up our bases.”

Zelensky’s immediate, unsparing pushback triggered outrage from Trump. He repeated a call for Ukraine to hold elections, with Zelensky pushing back that Russia’s refusal to halt strikes against the country makes it impossible to hold a contest. Ukraine is also under martial law, making it illegal under the country’s constitution to hold an election.

Zelensky’s pushback was echoed by Ukrainian opposition politician Kira Rudik, leader of the Golos party, underscoring the country’s unity on the global stage, despite domestic disagreements over the Ukrainian president’s leadership.

“We are acting according to Ukrainian constitution, and it’s up to no other leader than Ukrainian people who and when we will be electing,” she said in an interview with Sky News.

But Trump retaliated further by having U.S. officials over the weekend call European capitals and Kyiv, threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons delivery through Europe if Ukraine refuses to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

A European official confirmed to The Hill the pressure campaign, which was first reported by the Financial Times.

The majority of U.S.-supplied weapons to Ukraine are provided through European purchases of American munitions under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL).

PURL-supplied weapons and U.S. intelligence sharing make it possible for Ukraine to hit Russia’s energy infrastructure and other high-value targets deep in the country — a strategy Zelensky defends as crucial in the face of Russia’s energy warfare against Ukraine.

On Sunday, Trump announced a sudden energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, although the Kremlin has not confirmed it will abide by the agreement. Hours later, the Russian military continued firing at Ukrainian infrastructure, hitting a power plant in Kharkiv and a gas production facility.

Ukraine was apparently caught off guard by the news, but Zelensky has said the country is willing to halt strikes when Russia does.

“When we speak about energy ceasefire, it means only one thing, that they don’t attack our energy infrastructure, and we don’t respond on their energy infrastructure,” he said. “This is called energy ceasefire.”

Russian strikes against Ukraine’s electricity grid, on top of other civilian infrastructure, is an effort to plunge the country into cold and darkness with winter fast approaching.

Ukrainians endured Russian strikes the previous winter with ingenuity — filling hot water bottles to keep warm and adding extra blankets at home — on top of international and government assistance, providing generators and heating tents with charging stations for cellphones and electronics.

Ukraine is warning that Russia is escalating that strategy this winter to break Ukraine’s resolve in its defense. With the full-scale war now in its fourth year, Ukraine has seized important battlefield gains over Russia, which led to key assistance from Trump.

This includes the president’s offer over the summer to grant Ukraine rights to co-produce Patriot missile interceptors — key air defense munitions that have been depleted amid the U.S. war with Iran — and Trump’s greenlighting of the Russia sanctions bill, signing it into law in September.

But Putin is projecting Russian dominance on the battlefield over Ukraine in an effort to convince the Trump administration that Russia is in a strong position and that Ukraine must make concessions.

Putin’s analysis of the battlefield is “so far from reality as to resemble hallucinations,” the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) wrote in an analysis on Oct. 2, following a speech Putin gave at the Valdai Discussion Club the day before.

The ISW called Putin’s claims “absurd” and part of a cognitive warfare strategy to falsely portray Russian advances sweeping across the battlefield. The ISW added that it cannot determine whether Putin actually believes his claims or is relying on false information from briefers who are incentivized to provide a positive report.

A culture of lying is “deeply ingrained in the Russian military command structure,” the ISW wrote.

articles.title: NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked
articles.summary: NATO commander issues warning as European officials have called for vigilance over potential Russian attacks.
articles.body:
NATO’s top commander has warned that his forces would destroy “anything and everything” if someone was “foolish enough” to attack the alliance, as European concerns have mounted over a potential Russian attack on its territory amid the war in Ukraine.

“We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us,” US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, without mentioning Russia by name.

Grynkewich stressed that NATO is a defensive alliance and that he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable. The most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to “resolve misunderstandings”, he added.

European governments have accused Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Baltic Kaliningrad exclave where it has a major military outpost.

NATO’s 10-year strategy, created in 2022, described Russia as the alliance’s most significant security threat.

“We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile,” Grynkewich said.

Attacking anything that ‘supports, sustains and controls that force’

Grynkewich added that NATO’s response would not be limited to forces involved in an initial attack.

“Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” he said.

“This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls that force.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin said this month that Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully. Such declarations have not reassured European leaders, who cite similar statements by Russia before its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Moscow has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations.

Grynkewich said he had decided to talk publicly about NATO’s plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people around the alliance nervous.

“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it,” he said.

Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington’s commitment to the alliance , citing President Donald Trump’s reception at a NATO summit in Ankara in July.

“I was in the room and I felt the love,” he said.

articles.summary: In 1990, Matt Roloff and Amy Roloff purchased a 16-acre farm in Hillsboro, Oregon, for $185,000, hoping to create a rural home for their growing family.
articles.body: In 1990, Matt Roloff and Amy Roloff purchased a 16-acre farm in Hillsboro, Oregon, for $185,000, hoping to create a rural home for their growing family. Thirty-six years later, the property that became famous through TLC's Little People, Big World is embroiled in another family dispute. Matt's son Jacob Roloff and his wife, Isabel, fear they may have to leave the sprawling agricultural property after Matt allegedly indicated plans to sell the land. The couple, who live and work on the farm with their five-year-old son, Matteo, say the prospect of losing their home and farming operation has left them devastated.How Roloff Farms became a family landmarkWhen Matt and Amy bought the property in 1990, it was far from the picturesque attraction it would eventually become. The land had a rundown farmhouse and a rat-infested barn, but the couple saw an opportunity to build something special.Matt, who had worked as a computer programmer in California, spearheaded a major transformation of the property. He rebuilt the barn, created a mine shaft for children to explore, dug a pond featuring a full-sized pirate ship and acquired a vintage 1950s fire truck. The farm gradually became known for its unusual attractions and annual pumpkin season.In 2011, Matt and Amy expanded their holdings by purchasing another 91-acre parcel for $950,000, according to property records.The family farm entered the national spotlight in 2006, when TLC premiered Little People, Big World. The reality series followed the Roloffs' family life and their work running the farm, making the property a recognisable part of American reality television. The show concluded in 2024, but the farm continues to shape the family's story.A divorce changed the future of the family propertyRoloff Farms was the setting for several important family occasions, including the weddings of Matt and Amy's sons Jeremy and Zach. Jeremy married Audrey on the property in 2014, while Zach and Tori exchanged vows there the following year in front of nearly 200 guests.However, Matt and Amy's divorce in 2015 marked a turning point. Amy eventually sold her shares in the property to Matt in separate transactions in 2019 and 2020, leaving him with full ownership.The question of who would eventually take over the farm became a source of tension. In 2022, Matt put the 16-acre section containing the approximately 5,000-square-foot farmhouse on the market for $4 million. He said he wanted to reduce his responsibilities as he got older.The proposed sale became a major storyline on Little People, Big World. Both Jeremy and Zach reportedly made offers for the property, but Matt rejected them. The disagreements raised questions about whether the farm would remain within the family and how its legacy would continue.Why Jacob and Isabel Roloff are worried about losing their homeJacob and Isabel moved back to Roloff Farms in 2021, when they were expecting their first child. Under an arrangement with Matt, the couple rented a house on the property, Jacob earned a wage maintaining the farm, and Isabel cared for the animals.For a time, the arrangement appeared to be working. Isabel said the couple believed the part of the farm where they lived would not be sold.That understanding reportedly changed last month. In a TikTok video posted on September 15, Jacob suggested that he would likely no longer be living on the farm after January. In later posts, he appeared to indicate that Matt had told him he intended to sell the larger agricultural property.The prospect of leaving has been particularly difficult because the couple have built their home and farming activities there. They grow flowers, pumpkins and vegetables and care for animals on the land.“We see land as such a precious thing,” Isabel said. “We’ve been so grateful to live here, so we just feel devastated.”She added, “We’re still hoping for a miracle.”According to Isabel, she and Jacob have been told that they may need to move in January or February, although no final arrangements have been confirmed.Matt Roloff responds to the alleged sale plansMatt has addressed the dispute by saying that his focus is on retirement and treating his family fairly.In a statement to PEOPLE, he said, “I’m focused on my retirement plans and being fair to all my family members that I love and adore including all my grandchildren.”The publication reported that while the 16-acre section containing the farmhouse has been listed for sale on and off for around five years, the possibility of selling the larger agricultural land was new to Jacob and Isabel.Matt's response comes amid renewed questions about the future of the property, which has been closely associated with the family for decades. The disagreement has also revived concerns about how the farm's ownership will affect the next generation of Roloffs.Isabel says there is 'so much hurt and tension' within the familyThe latest dispute has emerged against a backdrop of complicated family relationships. Just three months earlier, Jacob had described his relationship with his family members as “normal” in an interview with PEOPLE. Isabel offered a different perspective on the tensions within the family.“I think that there’s just so much hurt and tension within the family,” she said.Reflecting on her position as someone who married into the Roloff family, she added, “As somebody who married into it, I’m very much like, ‘Can’t we all get along?’ But I can’t mend fences that I never broke.”Isabel also clarified that she and Jacob are not expecting Matt to give them the farm. Their wish, she said, is to continue living and working there if possible.“We just want to continue working and living here, if possible,” she told the publication.Jacob Roloff's complicated history with 'Little People, Big World'Jacob's relationship with the property is shaped by his experiences growing up in front of television cameras. He appeared on Little People, Big World as the youngest son of Matt and Amy when the series premiered in 2006.Over time, Jacob spoke publicly about difficult experiences during his childhood and his time on the show. He alleged that a producer had molested him and raised concerns about being fairly compensated for his participation. These remain allegations made by Jacob.After turning 18 in 2016, he left the series, moved away from the farm and stepped back from the spotlight. He later married Isabel in a ceremony away from television cameras, choosing to share aspects of his personal life on his own terms.His return to Roloff Farms in 2021 marked a new chapter. Isabel previously told PEOPLE that living there with their son had helped Jacob see the property differently and move forward from painful memories.She said being on the farm as a parent had felt like “new beginnings”, allowing him to experience the place through the eyes of his child.What lies ahead for Jacob and Isabel's farming operation?With the possibility of moving drawing closer, Jacob and Isabel are considering how they might continue their farming activities elsewhere. Finding a new property would mean not only relocating their household but also figuring out how to transport their animals and maintain their work.Isabel said buying another farm was not financially viable for them, despite suggestions from followers. The couple have also declined calls to launch a fundraiser, explaining that there are other causes more deserving of donations.For now, they are focusing on the farm's annual pumpkin season and continuing to welcome visitors.“We’re still encouraging people to come out because we still love the aspect of people coming out and seeing the beautiful farm,” Isabel said.She added, “We’ve loved our time here growing flowers, growing pumpkins, growing vegetables — it would just be sad to say goodbye.”You use AI every day. articles.title: A 67-year-old Maryland school bus driver was removed from her route after allowing a 10-year-old boy to step off and rescue a kitten; a petition seeking her reinstatement have  800 plus signatures
articles.summary: A 67-year-old school bus driver in Maryland has lost her route after allowing a 10-year-old student to rescue an injured kitten from the side of a rural
articles.body: A 67-year-old school bus driver in Maryland has lost her route after allowing a 10-year-old student to rescue an injured kitten from the side of a rural road, prompting parents and community members to campaign for her reinstatement. According to CBS News Baltimore, The Baltimore Sun and The Independent, the incident has sparked a debate over student safety, disciplinary action and the circumstances surrounding the driver’s removal. Cynthia Morgan, who has driven school buses for Harford County Public Schools (HCPS) for 11 years, was removed from her route earlier this week after the incident on Heaps School Road in Pylesville, Maryland. The decision has drawn criticism from families who say Morgan had built strong relationships with the children she transported over the years.What happened on the rural Maryland road?The incident occurred when 10-year-old Alex Thomas spotted a kitten on the roadside while travelling on Morgan’s school bus. According to The Baltimore Sun, Morgan stopped the vehicle and allowed the boy to retrieve the animal.Alex was the only student on the bus at the time. He carried the kitten with him until they reached North Harford Elementary School, after which Morgan took responsibility for the animal. The decision to let a child leave the bus has since become the central issue in the dispute. While some parents have argued that the rescue was a compassionate response to an animal in distress, others acknowledge that school transport safety rules exist to prevent potentially dangerous situations.Footage from the rural road, reviewed by CBS News Baltimore, showed little traffic at the location. However, the low-traffic conditions have not eliminated concerns about allowing a student to leave a school bus during a journey.Parents rally behind the longtime driverMorgan’s removal has prompted several parents to support her return, with a petition calling for her reinstatement attracting hundreds of signatures by October 9. Alex’s mother, Taffy Thomas, has backed the driver, saying her son would have been deeply upset if he had been unable to help the kitten. She believes the decision to remove Morgan has had an emotional impact on the child.Other parents have also highlighted Morgan’s longstanding involvement with students beyond her driving duties. Carolyn Kalambihis, whose three children travelled on Morgan’s bus for five years, described her as someone who regularly went out of her way to make children feel welcome. According to Kalambihis, Morgan purchased school supplies for students at the beginning of the academic year and gave them gifts during holidays and birthday cards on their special days, using her own money.Although parents have questioned the severity of the disciplinary action, some have also acknowledged the safety concerns raised by the incident. Their argument is that the matter could have been addressed through a different form of disciplinary action rather than removing a familiar and valued driver from her route.School district cites safety responsibilitiesHarford County Public Schools has maintained that student safety remains its priority. In statements reported by CBS News Baltimore and The Baltimore Sun, the district explained that decisions concerning the certification of school bus drivers can involve multiple circumstances and requirements rather than a single incident.The distinction is important because Morgan was employed by Cleary Transportation Inc., an independent contractor, rather than directly by the school district. HCPS is nevertheless responsible for certifying drivers who transport students on its behalf.A report by The Baltimore Sun also revealed that an October 5 letter from the district’s transportation director to the contractor referred to multiple incidents involving Morgan, including concerns about inappropriate interactions with students. The letter reportedly cited the kitten incident as part of the review of her certification.According to the report, the district reviewed footage of the journey and noted that Morgan had allowed the student to retrieve the kitten and subsequently kept the animal on board. Morgan maintained that she had not placed the child at risk and defended her actions during a meeting with district officials. The broader circumstances cited in the letter suggest that the decision may not have been based solely on the kitten rescue, although the district has not publicly detailed all the factors involved in Morgan’s case.Cleary Transportation directed media enquiries to the school district, while HCPS declined to discuss the individual driver’s certification status. As the petition continues to draw support, the dispute remains unresolved. For the families campaigning for Morgan’s return, the incident has raised questions about how school transport safety requirements are enforced and whether disciplinary decisions can account for the circumstances surrounding an individual case.You use AI every day. articles.title: Selma Blair arrested at JFK, then hospitalized after she attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane
articles.summary: Actor Selma Blair was arrested Sunday at John F Kennedy Airport in New York on allegations that she assaulted flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines
articles.body: Actor Selma Blair was arrested Sunday at John F Kennedy Airport in New York on allegations that she assaulted flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines flight. The Delta Air Lines flight 938 was parked at the gate when the incident allegedly happened. The flight reached JFK from Los Angeles. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said the 54-year-old actor was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation. FBI was investigating the allegations against Blair.A Delta spokesperson said to US media that the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”. The spokesperson added that Blair’s arrest did not affect the flight she and her fellow passengers were on – and that it still landed ahead of schedule at JFK.What exactly happened on the flightSeveral news outlets on Monday reported that Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open the airplane door.Her publicist told the Hollywood Reporter: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is [now] in stable condition.”TMZ reported that Selma has been charged with 2 counts of assault due to the alleged encounters with both the nurse and the officer.A pilot called for assistance during the flight in dispatch audio. “Could you pass on to the folks at JFK, we’d like to have some medical personnel at the gates for a couple of [flight attendants] involved in the passenger incident,” the pilot said in the recording, as cited by PageSix.“They just need to get a couple of things looked at,” he added.The pilot continued, “No ambulances. Just some medical personnel available for two flight attendants at the gate should be fine for that.”The pilot described the injuries as “A bloody nose as well as some bite marks.”The pilot then shared that the “disruptive passenger” had “bashed her head on the bulkhead” and would also need to be “potentially checked out as well as involved with law enforcement.”It was the second time Blair was reported to be involved in such an incident. In 2016, she reportedly began screaming uncontrollably before being removed on a stretcher while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico. Blair apologized after the earlier episode, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”.“That caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said at the time.You use AI every day. articles.title: What happened to missing Louisiana man Michael McLendon? Search continues nearly four months later
articles.summary: Michael McLendon was last seen on June 20, 2026, when he left the Sleep Inn & Suites in Pineville, Louisiana. The LaSalle Parish Sheriff’s Office is working with the Pineville Police Department to investigate his disappearance.
articles.body: “I’ve known Michael since he was 17,” Rena McLendon told Dateline. She’s been married to Michael’s brother for more than three decades. “So I’ve known Michael for a very, very long time.” Rena describes her brother-in-law as a caring person with a big heart. “He loved people, and he loved to help people,” she said. Over the years, Michael worked in oil fields and plants in the Deep South. “And then he became disabled, and hurt his back in one of the -- his jobs.” That didn’t stop Michael from helping his loved ones. “He was living with us,” Rena said. “I had a broken foot, so he would help me a lot around the house. He would take care of things that I couldn’t take care of.” In June 2026, Michael told Rena he wanted to get away for a bit. She says Michael told her he and his wife were going to stay in Pineville, Louisiana, about 45 minutes away from Jena, where he had been staying with Rena and her husband. “This is a really small town,” Rena said. “Everybody likes to know your business. So they just wanted to step away for a little while.” Then, he vanished. The 51-year-old was last seen on June 20, when he left the Sleep Inn & Suites in Pineville. Rena says she knew almost immediately that something was wrong when Michael stopped contacting the family. “Michael always stayed in contact with us,” she said. “He never went a day without talking to one of us.” A press release from the LaSalle Parish Sheriff’s Office (LPSO) states that, “According to his wife, McLendon left the hotel room sometime in the early morning of June 20, 2026, and has not been seen since.” The LPSO is working with the Pineville Police Department “in a joint effort to locate McLendon,” the release noted. Dateline spoke with LaSalle Parish Sheriff Lane Windham about Michael’s case. “We started checking his bank records, checking his social media accounts, checking his phone records, and the day that he disappeared, all of that ceased,” he said. “There was no more activity on his phone as far as texting, calling, social media, and his bank account has had no activity on it either.” Windham told Dateline that about a month after Michael disappeared, landscapers came across his dark green 2004 Ford Expedition in a ravine along a levee next to the Red River in the Alexandria-Pineville area. “They were over there cutting the grass, saw the vehicle, you know, went down to it,” Windham said. The car wasn’t the only thing found in the ravine. “Found the cellphone outside the vehicle,” Windham said. It was dead. “The screen was cracked. So we don’t know if the screen was cracked before, you know, and he was just using a cracked screen, or when he dropped it, it cracked then.” Michael’s wallet was inside the car. “That’s when they called the police. Police came over, saw that it was listed as a, uh, vehicle that was associated with a missing person,” Windham said. Authorities later found security footage showing Michael’s vehicle driving along the levee. “It looked like he backed down the levee or slid down the levee,” Windham told Dateline. “He was trying to go back up it, and the vehicle got stuck.” Authorities searched the area. “When they found the vehicle, they came in and went, you know, both directions,” Windham said. “Where that levee’s at, it runs the whole length, you know, of the river down there, and it’s thick. The woods are thick.” Windham says searchers used K9s to cover the area. “I know they went a long way down each side of the levee,” he said. “Didn’t find anything.” Windham says it’s possible Michael ended up in the river. “I’m not saying this is what happened, but, I mean, he could have conceivably gotten in that water.” Boats “went up and down, you know, just seeing if they saw something on the edges,” he said. “But as far as dragging the river itself, that would be almost impossible.” Rena is also concerned Michael might be in the river. “This is not like him, just to be gone,” she said. Rena spoke to Dateline on behalf of her husband, who she says is too emotional to discuss his brother’s disappearance. “We just need some kind of closure on the situation.” As the four-month anniversary of Micheal’s disappearance approaches, Rena told Dateline, “We don’t have very much hope that he’s alive.” Sheriff Windham shares her concern. “If he was still alive, by now he would’ve reached out to someone, or someone would have seen or heard something from him by now.”The LPSO is hoping people will come forward with specific sightings of Michael. “But it’s starting to get harder to do that because -- people’s memory,” Windham explained. “We don’t really have a lot of information, which is a shame.” Rena McLendon has turned to social media to spread the word about Michael’s disappearance. “Trying to get the word out there,” she said. “I had several people help me as well to try to share it.” She hopes the increased attention will encourage anyone with information to come forward. According to the LaSalle Parish Sheriff’s Office press release, Michael is 5’11” and weighs approximately 160 lbs., although his family believes his weight was much higher than that when he disappeared. He has blond hair, blue eyes, and multiple tattoos. If you have information about Michael’s whereabouts, please contact the LaSalle Parish Sheriff’s Office at 318-992-2151. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: A cross country runner switched to the girls team midseason, parents voice their disapproval at meet
articles.summary: A Camas High cross country runner switched from the boys team to the girls team midseason, sparking national debate over transgender athletes in sports.
articles.body: "Nobody wants to talk to you. I'm trying to be nice." That was the not-so-nice greeting I got from a Camas High assistant cross country coach in Arlington, Washington on Saturday. It came as I stood near the start line for the Women's Elite 5k race at the Nike Hole in the Wall High School XC Invitational. All I had done at that point was try to introduce myself, but it was clear that everybody involved with the school was on guard. The reason? One of the Camas runners entered in the Women's Elite 5K was a biological male. AMERICANS CLASH OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES AS DEBATE HEATS UP: ‘JUST GETTING OUTRAGEOUS' What's unique about this particular trans athlete is that he started the year on the boys team — with which he finished 76th in a JV race — then switched to the girls team last month. He has since taken first place in a varsity meet and finished second in a different invitational. This, as you might imagine, has sparked national attention, putting everyone at Camas on the defensive. But that assistant was wrong about one thing: Lots of people — mainly parents from opposing schools — wanted to talk to me. "We're about as liberal as it gets. I just don't agree with that [boys competing against girls]. I mean, if they find your body in 300 years, what are they going to say you were," said Kent Lake of Lake Stevens, WA. "Look, you can live any way you want. You got my blessing. But I mean come on, in competitions? It's like stock car racing. It's gotta be even, and it's gotta be fair." What prompted the Camas runner to switch from the boys to the girls team remains unclear. No Camas coach would talk (although one, along with a school administrator, was gracious to me), and the boy's mother wouldn't acknowledge my presence Saturday. WASHINGTON TRANS ATHLETE'S SCHOOL DISTRICT RESPONDS TO ALLEGED ASSAULT VICTIM'S SCOTUS INJUNCTION REQUEST But such a switch is permitted under the rules of the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA), which governs high school sports in the state. That doesn't mean most parents like it. "When I first heard about this story, I was like, 'Is this real? That can't be real'," said a mother of a cross country runner, who requested anonymity. She argued that allowing transgender runners to compete against girls could deprive female athletes of victories they otherwise would have earned. "We have daughters, and it's robbing them of an opportunity to compete." I LOST A STATE CHAMPIONSHIP TO A BOY. I REFUSE TO LOSE MY VOICE It should be noted that the Camas runner isn't a star, even among girls. He finished 39th in a field of 135 in Saturday's race with a time of 18:36.8. But had he run in the Men's Elite 5K, he would have placed last out of 159 runners by a good 30 seconds. Said one parent, also requesting anonymity. "Whether they finish first, 40th or 90th, they're still taking the spot of a girl." The anonymous route is the one that most chose last Saturday. One man wouldn't even let me record his voice — I had to repeat his quote into my phone using my own voice. This, after all, may be the most sensitive, contentious issue there is in sports. And ... not all the parents at Saturday's meet were necessarily against the Camas runner. One said, "People can identify however they want. High school sports isn't about winning, it's about student athletes building confidence." Another said, "There are more important things in sports than that [issue]." A third said, "I just wish people could have more empathy and compassion and understanding for people. I do think it's tricky if you start on one team and midseason change. I wish there was a space for everyone." Most, however, were like Kevin Ess, an Arlington High parent who had a compassionate but firm take on the matter. "I think men and women, young men and young women, have been competing for hundreds of years, thousands of years, separately," Ess said. "I think it's an interesting experiment. I think it's an interesting topic, but my personal opinion is that they should continue to compete separately." ATTORNEY FOR ALLEGED VICTIM OF TRANS ATHLETE SEXUAL ASSAULT SAYS SCOTUS FIGHT CAN HELP SET TITLE IX PRECEDENT One father said something similar after lifting his hoodie to reveal the XX-XY shirt he was sporting underneath. Another said allowing boys to compete with girls was "stupid" and that "Title IX was designed to protect women." A mother said, "I would be so embarrassed to put my son in a position like this." And though part of me agrees with that last part, part of me also wonders if it's a little harsh. I was genuinely curious about what the past few weeks have been like for the Camas runner's parents, but the mother completely ignored me on two separate attempts to talk. This was the same woman who reportedly started recording an athlete who protested the Camas runner last month by walking off the start line when the gun went off. That athlete was Skyview High junior Charlie Garrett, who staged the walk-off alongside teammate Sierra Retzlaff. Both wore body paint saying "Keep women in women's sports" that mid-September day — and both were on hand at Saturday's event as well. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "Why is it so important for you to speak out on this topic?" Retzlaff said: "Because if we don't, no one else will. If we start something, maybe others will have the courage to join." Fortunately, there have been other girls and women who have spoken on this issue from Washington state and beyond. In fact, such courage helped get Initiative 638 — which would ban biological males from competing against girls in K-12 sports — on the Nov. 3 ballot in Washington state. The situation in Camas could very well mobilize people to vote. People need to get out and vote for what they want."

articles.title: South Africa deputy police chief resigns amid sex offence charges
articles.summary: Shadrack Sibiya, who is in prison after his arrest last month, denies corruption, rape and child grooming allegations.
articles.body:
The deputy head of South Africa’s police has resigned amid allegations of corruption and rape, which he denies.

Shadrack Sibiya was set to face a disciplinary hearing on Monday, but his lawyers tendered his resignation at the start of proceedings.

In a post on social media platform X, a spokesperson said that Sibiya’s departure was regarded as a “dishonourable discharge” due to the ongoing disciplinary case against him.

He had been suspended since September last year.

Sibiya is currently in prison after he was arrested for the alleged rape and grooming of a minor last month. His application to be released on bail has been postponed to October 13.

The former deputy police chief has been the subject of a judicial commission of inquiry investigating allegations of corruption within the South African police and alleged ties to organised crime.

At the commission, Sibiya has been accused of receiving large sums of cash and gifts from alleged criminals, which he denied during his testimony.

articles.title: Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food
articles.summary: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers ​at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, causing fires and spoiling food.
articles.body: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers ​at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), causing fires and spoiling food. The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday ‌that a “large-scale” attack was “affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France,” leading to food losses and fires. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office said. France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk. Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 ​stores in France, said 5 per cent of its stores were affected. Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarche, said fridges at around 150 of its ⁠stores were heated up to 50 C for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said all affected food had been discarded to eliminate health risks. Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff ​at an Intermarche in central Paris throwing cartfuls of defrosted frozen foods into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street. Cooperative U CEO ​Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket group had also been targeted. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X. Food retailers E.Leclerc and Auchan did not respond to requests for comment. There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens ​of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.” Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said, “This incident underlines the importance of resilience across the entire supply chain.” Cold aisles controlled over internet Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere. The source ‌close to ⁠Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”. The affected units “were running outdated firmware,” Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions.” On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty’s Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass ​authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices. The ​attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a ⁠dozen US military commissaries in late August that led to food losses after fridges were affected. In a statement, French retail association Fédération du Commerce et de la Distribution called for “full transparency” from Danfoss about the incident. It said supermarkets aimed to protect consumers and return to ​normal operations as soon as possible. The FCD said some impacted stores were already back up and running. Dutch security issue Dutch retailer ​Ahold Delhaize, which operates the ⁠Netherlands’ largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a “security issue” on its network and had taken several systems offline as a precaution. A message on the retailer’s smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a “cybersecurity incident”. Online orders account for about 10 per cent of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news ⁠agency ANP ​reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders. Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to ​see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets. Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying “site temporarily down”.

articles.title: Why do Iran’s oil ‘intermediaries’ owe the government billions?
articles.summary: Iran says intermediaries handling its oil sales owe it billions of dollars, but how did the debts accumulate?
articles.body:
As the United States maintains a naval blockade of Iran’s ports and imposes more sanctions on its oil exports, Tehran is confronting another problem: billions of dollars in revenue from previous oil sales that it says have gone missing.

A spokesperson for Iran’s judiciary said in September that a network of oil intermediaries known as “trustees” owed the Iranian government between 10 billion euros ($11bn) and 11 billion euros ($12bn). That figure was equivalent to half of the total oil revenue projected in Iran’s government budget for the current fiscal year.

US officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, have tied Iran’s struggles to access oil revenues as evidence that its economic pressure campaign is having an effect. In August, Bessent said that “Iran’s shadow banking system was buckling” under pressure from the US campaign against the country, which has been ramped up as Washington seeks a way to force Tehran to capitulate in the war between the two countries, launched by the US and Israel in late February.

So who are the oil intermediaries, why does Iran depend on them, and what has happened to the billions of dollars they owe? Let’s take a closer look.

The debt, and the crisis it has created for the Iranian government, both stem from an oil-sales arrangement Tehran adopted in 2012 in response to US sanctions targeting Iranian oil exports.

American and European sanctions targeting Iranian oil sales and revenue collection began in 2012. The stated rationale behind both sets of measures was that revenue from oil sales helped finance Iran’s nuclear programme and that restricting Iranian oil exports could prevent the programme from advancing.

In response, the Iranian government devised a way to circumvent international sanctions on its oil sales. Unable to sell oil through the Oil Ministry and receive the proceeds through the Central Bank, it began selling oil to domestic buyers or using it to settle outstanding obligations to institutions and organisations owed money by the state.

This arrangement gave rise to a network of oil intermediaries often referred to in Iran as the “trustee network”. Rather than selling all its oil through official government channels, the state entrusted crude oil to institutions, individuals and companies to sell on its behalf. The proceeds were supposed to be transferred to the government’s treasury, with the sellers or recipient institutions subsequently recovering their agreed costs and outstanding claims. Some institutions sold the oil themselves, while others contracted private trading companies to handle the sales.

The Oil Industry Pension Fund, established for retired Oil Ministry employees familiar with the oil-sales process, was among the first institutions to receive crude oil for sale. Other recipients included Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Base, a major hub for large-scale infrastructure projects. Even the municipal police received payments owed to them by the government in the form of crude oil.

Even in those early experiments, discrepancies emerged between the revenue expected from oil sales and the amounts sellers actually deposited into the government’s treasury. These discrepancies eventually gave rise to some of Iran’s largest economic corruption cases.

The accounting discrepancies and the government’s inability to recover money from private sellers entrusted with Iranian oil persisted until 2016, when the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) nuclear deal was signed and when sanctions on Iranian oil sales were lifted. The government was subsequently able to regain control over oil sales.

Individuals who had sold Iranian oil but failed to return the proceeds were imprisoned. With the ability to sell oil again through legal and transparent channels, the government was able, for a time, to manage its oil revenues and spending with greater control.

How did money from oil sales go unreturned?

After US President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from the JCPOA in 2018 during his first presidential term, the Iranian government once again had to rely on private oil traders to sell its oil. But the problems associated with selling oil through intermediaries rather than official state channels, including delays in returning revenues, accounting discrepancies, debts owed by oil sellers to the government, and the occasional seizure of Iranian oil shipments at sea, once again constrained the government’s ability to manage its oil revenues.

Moreover, the US expanded its sanctions beyond Iranian government institutions and interests, adding bank accounts involved in transactions with the Iranian government, currency-exchange offices, companies, and individuals to its sanctions lists. As a result, the time between individuals participating in Iran’s oil-trading network and being sanctioned themselves, along with their assets and companies, and having their accounts blocked or frozen grew progressively shorter.

This contributed to an accumulation of debts owed by sanctioned oil traders – no longer able to access their accounts – to the government. It also left Iran with little choice but to expand its private oil-sales network. That meant increasing the number of people involved in trading Iranian oil, reducing the volume of oil allocated to each individual or company and, ultimately, increasing the risk that the proceeds would not be returned.

Iranian officials have also accused trustees of exploiting the sanctions workarounds to enrich themselves .

The billions of dollars owed by private oil sellers to the Iranian government are a combination of outstanding payments, disputed financial obligations and allegations of corruption. Iran’s judiciary chief recently addressed the issue, warning that oil sellers who refuse to return the proceeds from oil sales will face legal action. But such warnings do not change the sanctions environment or remove the obstacles that prevent some oil sellers from returning the money.

articles.title: Canada’s Carney calls for unity as Alberta prepares for secession vote
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Thanksgiving message comes a week ahead of Alberta’s referendum to secede.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has used his Thanksgiving message to Canadians to call for national unity, a week before the oil-rich province of Alberta is set to vote on a proposal to secede from Canada.

“We can’t build big things on fault lines,” Carney said in his video message on Monday, warning that Canada faces threats to its economy, security and way of life.

“We have to be strong, and we are stronger together.”

His comments come as Albertans head to the polls on October 19 to decide whether to begin the process of seeking independence. The initial referendum is non-binding, but it proposes to hold a binding vote in the future to decide whether Alberta should secede.

The question facing voters is: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

The vote follows a growing push by a vocal group of separatists, fuelled by longstanding grievances over federal energy and environmental policies.

The secessionist movement has accused the Canadian government of unfairly targeting Alberta’s oil and gas industry, the cornerstone of the province’s economy.

The movement is also being watched south of the border, as Canada’s relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump has become strained.

An investigation by The Globe and Mail earlier this month revealed that US Republican operatives met with secession organisers in Alberta to talk about campaign strategies. Separatist leaders had reportedly offered access to the province’s water and oil royalties in exchange for US support for independence. Separatist leaders have disputed those claims.

Carney’s comments also come after another secessionist movement, the Parti Quebecois, won the most seats in a provincial election in Quebec last week, allowing it to return to power after more than a decade.

The Parti Quebecois, however, only won 59 seats out of a total of 129 in Quebec’s National Assembly, leaving it short of a majority government.

Still, following that victory, US tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, considered the richest man on the planet, applauded the results. He has been known to use his wealth and influence to support political causes, particularly on the far right.

“Good. Quebec should separate,” Musk wrote on social media. “They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, said he was filming the message from a classroom at his former school, St Francis Xavier High School in Edmonton.

“I’m back home a lot these days because we are building big things again in Alberta: thousands of new homes, high-speed rail, a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity for hundreds of thousands of people in this province and across the country,” he said.

Despite the secessionist movement’s growing visibility, polls suggest most Albertans oppose independence.

articles.title: On cracker ban, SC says mustn't pass orders difficult to enforce
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Aware of the flagrant violation of its past Diwali cracker ban order which had specified time windows for bursting green crackers, Supreme
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Aware of the flagrant violation of its past Diwali cracker ban order which had specified time windows for bursting green crackers, Supreme Court on Monday refused to consider strict control over bursting of crackers and said the court must not pass orders which are difficult to implement on the ground."We have to be extremely careful in passing an order, which must be manageable and enforceable," a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said. This came in response to amicus curiae and senior advocate Aparajita Singh's plea that there could not be carte blanche for cracker bursting which, apart from causing serious pollution, adversely impacted the health of children, senior citizens and patients.The bench said, "The best way is to make people wiser, awaken them about harmful crackers and motivate them to exercise self-restraint while persuading them to return to the original tradition of lighting lamps. But sale of harmful crackers must be stopped."When the amicus said worship was part of religion and not firecrackers, and that gods would be aghast if they found that children were being harmed because of cracker bursting in their name, the bench responded, "We will not hurt religious sentiments. But at the same time, we are for the creation of an appropriate atmosphere through education and persuasion to enable people to exercise self-restraint."Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati said the regime of green crackers was already the SC's mandate. The blanket ban on cracker bursting was modified last year allowing sale of green crackers for two days and bursting for another two-day window.When the amicus focused on adverse impacts of cracker bursting, SC said, "The moment we pass a restricting order, people will take it as coercive action and react differently. We must be very practical and pragmatic in such issues. There is sufficient time for the govt to disseminate information about harmful effects of crackers and persuade them to limit it to bare minimum."Justice Bagchi said the primary concerns were health and pollution. "What will be the pollution load if people burst crackers in a short period of time?" he asked. The amicus suggested that the issue should be referred to the Commission on Air Quality Management (CAQM), which could examine the issue with the help of experts and give its suggestions to the court for passing appropriate orders.Cracker manufacturers represented by senior advocate K Parameshwar and Sai Deepak said CAQM's report could be sought on the issue. Amicus said the right to religion and right to health needed balancing as petitioners argued the right to religion every time.The court also touched upon issue of stubble burning, which has engaged the SC's attention for the last few years, and said stubble converted into bales had become commercially viable and required state support to enable farmers to shift from stubble burning.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
